notes: Appeal by case stated on s 172 RTA 1988 driver identification; full judgment supports enrichment.

enrichment.short_title: Section 172 driver identification and written response by letter
key_facts: Dr Jones, keeper of a practice fleet vehicle, was caught speeding in Cardiff but could not identify which authorised driver was at the wheel.
He returned the s 172 notice with a signed covering letter explaining he was not the driver and could not ascertain who was, rather than completing the form boxes.
A deputy district judge convicted him of failing to give driver information, treating his response as non-compliant and damaging his credibility under DPP v Broomfield.
On appeal by case stated, the Divisional Court held a signed written letter cross-referred to the form was substantial compliance with s 172(2).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' court conviction to the Administrative Court (Divisional Court).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted with direction to acquit; costs of £1,450 ordered from central funds.
enrichment.ratio: A vehicle keeper who responds in writing by signed letter cross-referred to a s 172 notice substantially complies with the statutory requirement to give driver information; an adverse credibility finding based on erroneous insistence that only the prescribed form could be used cannot sustain conviction where the defence under s 172(4) turns on that credibility.
legal_issues: Whether a signed covering letter satisfies s 172(2) Road Traffic Act 1988
Whether the deputy district judge erred in applying DPP v Broomfield to Dr Jones's written response
Whether the s 172(4) defence was properly rejected on credibility grounds
linked_authorities: DPP v Broomfield [2002] EWHC 1962 (Admin)
Boss v Measures (1990) RTR 26

confidence.notes: Single clear ratio on form of compliance and credibility; outcome and statutory provisions explicit.

notes: Short written family appeal on Protocol party-status at transfer; enrichment from full text.

enrichment.short_title: Family Proceedings Court refusal to join grandparents at care transfer
key_facts: Maternal grandparents cared for child G from May 2003 during local authority care proceedings governed by the Public Law Children Act Protocol.
On transfer to the county court the FPC refused their application to be joined as parties and made an interim care order removing G to foster care without hearing them.
The justices relied on Protocol para 2.5 limiting FPC directions on transfer except as agreed for the care centre.
The grandparents argued the combined refusal breached their right to a fair hearing under the Protocol's overriding objective.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the High Court (Family Division) from a family proceedings court decision on party status and interim care at transfer under the Protocol.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the point of principle; no further order as grandparents were later heard in the care centre.
enrichment.ratio: The Protocol is a practical case-management tool subordinate to the Children Act and its Practice Direction; where transfer to a care centre coincides with a serious interim removal application, the FPC must either defer the application, determine party status, or permit intervention—rigid application of para 2.5 that excludes a directly affected carer is inconsistent with the overriding objective of dealing with cases justly and fairly.
legal_issues: Whether Protocol para 2.5 prevented the FPC from determining party status before transfer
Whether refusing to hear grandparents before an interim removal order breached fairness and the Protocol's purpose
The status and limits of the Public Law Children Act Protocol

confidence.notes: Principle and outcome clearly stated; Protocol cited by paragraph rather than statutory rule numbers.

notes: Trading standards fire safety prosecution appeal; detailed findings on test methodology.

enrichment.short_title: Foam cushion ignitability test reliability in trading standards prosecution
key_facts: PR Manufacturing Ltd supplied garden relaxer chair cushions that failed BTTG Wiratec ignitability tests after trading standards test purchases.

The company was convicted on false trade description counts but acquitted on Consumer Protection Act counts because justices preferred the defendant's density-by-calculation test method over Wiratec's manual 'feel' method.
Justices found Wiratec's test complied with the Regulations yet also that the prosecution result could not be relied on—a finding the judge held inconsistent.
The prosecution appealed by case stated on whether the ignitability evidence was sufficient for conviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates to the High Court (Administrative Court) by the prosecutor.
enrichment.outcome: Not guilty verdicts on the two Consumer Protection Act informations set aside; matter remitted to a differently constituted bench for retrial.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates find that a prosecution ignitability test was performed in accordance with the 1988 Regulations and that the supplier breached reg 6(2)(b), it is inconsistent and an error of law to acquit because a different private test method produced a pass result; absent evidence of procedural failure in the prosecution test, a failed approved test engages reg 15 and s 12(1) CPA 1987.
legal_issues: Reliability of manual 'feel' versus calculated density methods under Sch 1 Pt II
Whether justices could reject prosecution expert evidence without adequate reasons
Whether comparison with later defendant-initiated tests on different cushions was permissible
Consistency of findings that tests complied with the Regulations with acquittal on CPA charges
linked_authorities: Lucie M v Worcestershire CC [2002] EWHC Admin 1292

confidence.notes: Core inconsistency finding and regulatory chain clearly explained; some procedural sub-issues answered briefly.

notes: Introductory tenancy possession judicial review; Forbes and McLellan considered.

enrichment.short_title: Introductory tenancy s 128 notice and additional nuisance grounds
key_facts: Newham sought possession of Miss Laporte's introductory tenancy for rent and water charge arrears and later antisocial behaviour by her son.
A s 128 notice cited rent arrears; before review Newham added nuisance allegations and confirmed possession after review and a meeting without serving a fresh s 128 notice.
Miss Laporte challenged reliance on grounds not in the original notice and on post-review nuisance incidents not put to her, including one wrongly attributed to her son.
Possession proceedings had begun in the county court while this judicial review was pursued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local authority decision to confirm pursuit of possession of an introductory tenancy following s 128 review.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; relief withheld in discretion despite technical procedural defects; leave to appeal refused; local authority awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where additional possession grounds are introduced after a s 128 notice, a fresh notice specifying those grounds may strictly be required and review should be confined to stated reasons; however, where the tenant received details, was heard on review and at a meeting, and valid rent arrears alone justified possession, refusal of relief for procedural non-compliance causing no material prejudice is within the court's discretion.
legal_issues: Whether nuisance grounds added after s 128 notice required a further notice and review
Whether post-review reliance on new nuisance allegations was unlawful
Compliance with Articles 6 and 8 in the introductory tenancy scheme
Whether Forbes v Lambeth and Cardiff City Council v Stone govern implementation of an extant s 128 decision
linked_authorities: R (McLellan) v Bracknell Forest Borough Council [2002] QB 1129
Forbes v London Borough of Lambeth [2003] EWHC 222 (Admin)
Cardiff City Council v Stone [2003] EWCA Civ 298

confidence.notes: Outcome turns on discretion and prejudice; substantive s 128 analysis largely obiter but clearly recorded.

notes: Companies Act change of name enforcement appeal; Patten and Lightman orders set aside.

enrichment.short_title: Court power to change company names after passing-off judgment
key_facts: Halifax obtained judgment against Mr Gopee for trademark infringement and passing off by companies using 'Halifax' in their names.
Patten J ordered the Registrar of Companies to change the companies' names; Lightman J later authorised a Halifax solicitor to procure name changes when Mr Gopee did not comply.
Names were ultimately changed pursuant to Lightman J's order, but Mr Gopee appealed on whether the court had power to effect changes otherwise than by special resolution.
Members of the companies were Mr Gopee's children and were not joined as parties to the name-change applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against High Court orders enforcing a change of registered company names following an IP judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; Patten J's and Lightman J's costs orders set aside; no order for costs on the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Order 45 rule 8 does not authorise the court to change a registered company's name except by a special resolution passed in accordance with the Companies Act 1985; nor may the court direct the Registrar of Companies to alter the register without the statutory resolution procedure and issue of a certificate of incorporation on change of name.
legal_issues: Whether Ord 45 r 8 permits court-ordered name change without member special resolution
Whether the Registrar of Companies may be directed to change a name on the register
Whether members or subscribers must be joined and mandatory orders made against them first
Whether Hoffmann J in Ford Sellar Morris and Jacob J in Barros Mattos support collapsing Ord 45 r 8 stages
linked_authorities: Ford Sellar Morris Developments Ltd v Grant Seward Ltd [1985] 29 EG 68
Luiz Vicente Barros Mattos Junior v Macdaniels Ltd [2002] EWHC 1547 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and appeal outcome explicit; collapsed-stage question left open obiter.

notes: Long preliminary-issues judgment on offshore platform contracts; enrichment summarises main holdings only.

enrichment.short_title: Petromec v Petrobras preliminary issues on P-36 upgrade contracts
key_facts: Petromec upgraded semi-submersible platform P-36 for Petrobras/Brasoil under complex bareboat charter and upgrade agreements originally framed for South Marlim but executed after the project shifted to Roncador.
Petromec claimed additional Roncador costs; Petrobras counterclaimed for delay; the court tried preliminary issues on the contractual framework before quantification.
Key documents included a 1996 MOA, June 1997 South Marlim agreements, an August 1998 Supervision Agreement, variation letters, and Deeds of Payment and Confirmation.
Disputes centred on whether Petromec bore performance risk, entitlement under Supervision Agreement cl 12, and finality of July 1998 and later settlement documents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of preliminary issues by consent in a claim for additional upgrade costs and a counterclaim for delay.
enrichment.outcome: On preliminary issues: MOA not binding; Petromec not liable for delay/defects once approved sub-contracts were placed; Supervision Agreement cl 12 entitles recovery of reasonable extra Roncador costs without extra profit; several alleged global settlements and indemnities held not to create further payment rights.
enrichment.ratio: The November 1996 MOA was a non-binding framework only; under the June 1997 upgrade structure Petromec performed by entering Brasoil-approved sub-contracts and did not assume liability for delay or defective work, while the Supervision Agreement cl 12 separately entitles Petromec to reasonable additional costs of the Roncador specification but not additional profit, and later variation and deed documents fixed or precluded further claims on the issues decided.
legal_issues: Whether the Memorandum of Agreement created enforceable obligations
Allocation of upgrade performance and delay risk under the South Marlim and Supervision agreements
Construction of Supervision Agreement clauses 9, 10 and 12 on Roncador changes and compensation
Whether July 1998, DPI, DCI and 1999 global settlement negotiations bound Petrobras to pay further sums
linked_authorities: Prenn v Simmonds [1971] 1 WLR 1381

confidence.notes: Very long judgment with nineteen numbered preliminary conclusions; enrichment compresses holdings and quantum remains for later trial.

notes: Short procedural judgment following Tasyurdu on notifying settled appeals.

enrichment.short_title: Duty to notify Civil Appeals Office when appeal settles late
key_facts: Employment Appeal Tribunal appeal listed for up to two days was settled at about 9am on the morning of hearing after agreement late the previous Friday.
Counsel and solicitors had not notified the Civil Appeals Office during negotiations or over the weekend despite Tasyurdu v SSHD [2003] EWCA Civ 447.
Judges had prepared over the weekend for a hearing that would not proceed.
The court recorded the profession's obligation to alert the court promptly when a fixture may not be effective.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal judgment on withdrawal of settled employment appeal and wasted preparation costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal withdrawn by consent; respondent's costs assessed under CLS Costs Regulations; no other costs order.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 1.3 parties and their lawyers must help the court use resources appropriately by informing the Civil Appeals Office as soon as it is known that a listed appeal will not proceed or is subject to serious settlement negotiations, including via the RCJ switchboard out of hours where necessary.
legal_issues: Professional duty following late settlement of a listed Court of Appeal employment appeal
Application of Tasyurdu guidance on notifying the Civil Appeals Office
Appropriate costs order on consent withdrawal
linked_authorities: Tasyurdu v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 447

confidence.notes: Brief procedural ratio clearly stated; no substantive employment merits decided.

notes: Leading boundary agreement analysis on s 2 LP(MP)A 1989; Neilson v Poole applied.

enrichment.short_title: Oral boundary agreement and section 2 writing requirement
key_facts: Mrs Joyce sold part of her garden as 7 Chanton Drive but the transfer plan did not fix the boundary with sufficient precision.
Mr Rigolli built a fence and garage; neighbours disputed whether they encroached on Mrs Joyce's retained land.
The county court judge found the paper title boundary unascertainable and upheld an oral November 2000 boundary agreement pegged out with a kink around a cherry tree.
Mrs Joyce appealed contending the agreement required writing under s 2 and conflicted with expert and witness evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from county court boundary trespass judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; boundary agreement upheld; appellant ordered to pay £1,500 costs.
enrichment.ratio: An informal boundary agreement that demarcates an unclear line on the ground rather than consciously conveying land is presumed not to be a contract for the disposition of an interest in land under s 2(1) LP(MP)A 1989; trivial conscious transfers pursuant to such agreements are de minimis, and proprietary estoppel may alternatively prevent s 2 applying where the agreement was acted upon.
legal_issues: Whether the boundary could be fixed from the registered title plan
Whether an oral demarcating boundary agreement complies with s 2(1) LP(MP)A 1989
Application of Neilson v Poole demarcation versus conveyance distinction
Whether the judge's findings on the agreed boundary line were open on the evidence
linked_authorities: Neilson v Poole (1969) 20 P&CR 909
Scarfe v Adams [1981] 1 All ER 843
Yaxley v Gotts [2000] Ch 162
Kingston v Phillips [1976] (unreported CA)

confidence.notes: Detailed ratio on s 2 and boundary agreements; fact findings largely upheld on appeal.

notes: Police Appeals Tribunal standard of review; Secretary of State guidance held ultra vires in part.

enrichment.short_title: Police Appeals Tribunal full merits appeal not Wednesbury review
key_facts: PC Hopes was required to resign after disciplinary findings on falsifying pocket notebook entries about an informant and breaching a lawful order not to contact him.
The Police Appeals Tribunal substituted a financial penalty, treating the sanction as unreasonable.
The Chief Constable sought judicial review arguing the tribunal should apply Wednesbury reasonableness review per Secretary of State guidance para 5.24.
Collins J held the tribunal is an independent expert appeal body with power to rehear and substitute its own sanction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Police Appeals Tribunal decision substituting a lesser disciplinary sanction.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; tribunal decision upheld; leave to appeal refused; interested party PC Hopes awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: A police appeals tribunal under s 85 Police Act 1996 conducts a full merits appeal, not Wednesbury review; it may hear fresh evidence and impose any lesser sanction available to the original decision-maker, and Secretary of State guidance under s 87 cannot lawfully require a reasonableness-only standard because tribunals are outside the guidance's statutory recipients.
legal_issues: Whether Police Appeals Tribunal review is Wednesbury or merits-based
Whether Secretary of State guidance para 5.24 binds the tribunal
Whether substitution of a financial penalty for required resignation was open
Proper burden and approach to mitigation in police misconduct sentencing
linked_authorities: Lothbury Investment Corporation Ltd v Inland Revenue Commissioners [1981] 1 Ch 47
Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation [1948] 1 KB 223
Stepney Borough Council v Joffe [1948] 1 KB 599

confidence.notes: Statutory framework and standard of review clearly decided; operational sentencing factors noted obiter.

notes: Detailed assessment after CA remittal; final figure £500,000 on dual time/value billing.

enrichment.short_title: Estate administration solicitors' dual basis costs assessment
key_facts: Kippax Beaumont Lewis billed £592,983.40 (excluding disbursements) for administering Sir Geoffrey Hulton's estate, combining hourly rates and a value element.

Residuary beneficiary Jemma Trust challenged 79 bills; the costs judge initially disallowed separate value charges but the Court of Appeal in [2003] EWCA Civ 1476 permitted dual billing subject to overall fairness.
The estate remained unwound ten years after death amid disputes with beneficiary Mr Butterfield and guardian Major Reynolds.
After reviewing files and witness evidence, the judge assessed fair remuneration at £500,000 total including a reduced value element.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment of solicitors' non-contentious probate bills following Court of Appeal remittal (costs judgment No. 2).
enrichment.outcome: Bills assessed at £500,000 fair and reasonable total (£358,093.29 after 5% time reduction plus £141,906.71 value element); below the £592,983.40 claimed.
enrichment.ratio: Non-contentious probate remuneration must be 'fair and reasonable' under the 1994 Order considering all para 3 factors; solicitors may charge both time and a separate value element provided there is no double recovery, the updated Maltby regressive scale is guidance not determinative, and overall remuneration reflects complexity, skill, estate value, and the extra work caused by difficult beneficiaries without penalising executors for delay they did not cause.
legal_issues: Application of Court of Appeal guidance on dual time and value billing after Jemma Trust
Whether assessment must await final estate winding-up
Allowance for unrecorded time and duplication between executor-solicitor and fee earner
Appropriate value element where Maltby-scale figure (£30,300) was far below claimed value charges
linked_authorities: Jemma Trust Co Ltd v Liptrott [2003] EWCA Civ 1476
Maltby v D J Freeman & Co (a firm)
Pesskin v Mishcon de Reya [2003] EWHC 1745 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Final assessed figure clear but reasoning spans many objections; related bills and negligence proceedings outside this assessment.
